Compare mortality-to-incidence ratios across registries

Source: R/compare_mi.R
compare_mi.Rd

compare_mi() applies the statistical test described by Parkin and Bray (2009) to identify registry mortality-to-incidence (M:I) ratios that differ from comparison registries. Each registry is tested in turn, using all other registries in the same stratum as its comparison population.

Usage

compare_mi(x, alpha = 0.05, reference = NULL)

Arguments

x

An object with class quality or qualities containing the registry identifier regicode, incident case counts fbs, and death counts sws.

alpha

A single numeric significance level strictly between 0 and 1. Defaults to 0.05, corresponding to a chi-squared critical value of approximately 3.84 with one degree of freedom.

reference

An optional external reference table. It must contain regicode, fbs, and sws; registry and cases are accepted as aliases for regicode and fbs. At least two reference rows are needed in each matched stratum to estimate dispersion.

Value

A tibble containing the stratum identifiers, regicode, fbs, sws, the observed mi, the number of comparison registries reference_n, the estimated common ratio theta, the dispersion estimate phi, the test statistic z2, p_value, critical_value, the logical flag unusual, and an evaluation status.

Details

The function accepts either the merged quality data frame returned by create_quality(..., collapse = TRUE) or the qualities list returned by create_quality(..., collapse = FALSE). Strata are detected automatically from identifier columns such as year, sex, and cancer.

By default, each registry is compared with the other registries in its stratum. Supply reference to use an external reference table instead. External rows are matched to each target stratum using the stratum columns shared by x and reference. For comparison registries indexed by \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), let \(d_i\) be the number of incident cases, \(m_i\) the number of deaths, and \(n_i = m_i + d_i\). The common M:I ratio and dispersion are estimated as $$\hat{\theta} = \frac{\sum_i m_i}{\sum_i d_i}$$ and $$\hat{\phi} = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_i \frac{(m_i - \hat{\theta}d_i)^2}{n_i\hat{\theta}}.$$ For the registry under test, indexed by \(j\), the statistic is $$Z^2 = \frac{(m_j - \hat{\theta}d_j)^2} {\hat{\phi}n_j\hat{\theta}}$$, which is compared with a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.

A status other than "ok" indicates that the row could not be evaluated. Possible values are "zero_target_incidence", "insufficient_reference_registries", "zero_reference_incidence", "zero_reference_mi", and "zero_reference_dispersion". An unusual result indicates a statistical difference from the comparison registries; it does not by itself establish incomplete registration.

References

Parkin, D. M., & Bray, F. (2009). Evaluation of data quality in the cancer registry: Principles and methods Part II. Completeness. European Journal of Cancer, 45(5), 756-764. doi:10.1016/j.ejca.2008.11.033

Examples

quality_data <- structure(
  data.frame(
    regicode = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
    year = "2024",
    sex = "1",
    cancer = "101",
    fbs = c(100, 100, 150, 200),
    sws = c(80, 40, 75, 80)
  ),
  class = c("quality", "data.frame")
)
compare_mi(quality_data)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 15
#>   regicode year  sex   cancer   fbs   sws    mi reference_n theta   phi     z2
#>   <chr>    <chr> <chr> <chr>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>       <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 A        2024  1     101      100    80   0.8           3 0.433 0.788 21.9  
#> 2 B        2024  1     101      100    40   0.4           3 0.522 6.19   0.330
#> 3 C        2024  1     101      150    75   0.5           3 0.5   7.14   0    
#> 4 D        2024  1     101      200    80   0.4           3 0.557 4.82   1.31 
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: p_value <dbl>, critical_value <dbl>, unusual <lgl>,
#> #   status <chr>
